title: IVF vs ICSI — Which Treatment Is Right For You?
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: IVF vs ICSI — what is the difference and which should you choose? Dr. Ankita Mandal explains both treatments clearly. Maatritva IVF, Newtown Kolkata.

content.h1: IVF vs ICSI — Which Fertility Treatment Is Right For You?
content.intro: When couples first hear about IVF and ICSI, the terms often blur together. Both involve fertilising eggs in a lab. But the key difference is significant — and choosing the right one can directly impact your success rate.
content.body:
IVF (In Vitro Fertilisation) places thousands of sperm around each egg in a lab dish and allows natural fertilisation to occur. This works well when sperm quality is normal or near-normal.

ICSI (Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection) goes one step further: a single carefully selected sperm is injected directly into each mature egg. This is essential when:
- Sperm count is very low (below 5 million/mL)
- Sperm motility is severely compromised
- Previous IVF cycles had poor or zero fertilisation
- Sperm is surgically retrieved (TESA/PESA)
- Sperm DNA fragmentation is high

At Maatritva IVF in Newtown, Kolkata, Dr. Ankita Mandal recommends ICSI in any situation where fertilisation may be at risk — it adds only a small cost but significantly improves the fertilisation guarantee.

For couples with unexplained infertility and normal semen parameters, standard IVF may be recommended first. But if fertilisation is suboptimal after one cycle, ICSI is adopted immediately.

The bottom line: IVF and ICSI share the same stimulation, egg retrieval, and transfer steps. The only difference is how the egg is fertilised in the lab. Your embryologist and Dr. Ankita will always recommend the approach most likely to give you a healthy embryo — and explain exactly why.
content.conclusion: Whether you need IVF or ICSI, the most important factor is an experienced team that personalises your protocol. At Maatritva IVF, we review every semen analysis individually before deciding. Book a free consultation to discuss your specific case.

title: IVF Success Rates by Age in India — Honest Numbers Explained
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal

content.h1: IVF Success Rates by Age in India — What the Numbers Actually Mean
content.intro: You will see clinics claiming '70% success rates' everywhere. But success rates mean nothing without context — specifically, your age and the type of embryo transferred. Here is an honest breakdown.
content.body:
IVF success rates depend primarily on the woman's age at egg retrieval — because egg quality declines with age.

Approximate live birth rates per embryo transfer (own eggs):
- Under 35: 55–70%
- Age 35–37: 45–55%
- Age 38–40: 35–45%
- Age 41–42: 20–35%
- Age 43+: 10–20% (own eggs); 55–65% with donor eggs

With PGT-A (preimplantation genetic testing), only chromosomally normal embryos are transferred — this significantly improves success rates per transfer at all ages, particularly over 37.

At Maatritva IVF in Newtown, Kolkata, Dr. Ankita Mandal is committed to giving every patient honest expectations before treatment begins. We do not inflate statistics. We give you YOUR numbers based on your AMH, antral follicle count, age, and diagnosis.

The key distinction: pregnancy rate vs live birth rate. A clinic quoting a 'pregnancy rate' includes chemical pregnancies and early losses. The live birth rate — a baby you actually take home — is always lower and is the only number that truly matters to you.

For women over 40 with low reserve, the conversation about donor eggs is approached compassionately and without pressure. Dr. Ankita always puts your informed decision first.
content.conclusion: Ask any clinic you consult: what is your live birth rate, broken down by age group? If they cannot answer — that is itself an answer. At Maatritva IVF, we believe transparency builds trust.

title: PCOS Diet for Fertility — What to Eat to Improve Your Chances
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: PCOS diet tips for fertility from Dr. Ankita Mandal at Maatritva IVF Kolkata. Evidence-based foods that improve ovulation, insulin resistance, and IVF outcomes with PCOS.

content.h1: PCOS Diet for Fertility — What Dr. Ankita Recommends Her Patients Eat
content.intro: Nutrition is not a replacement for treatment — but for women with PCOS, the right dietary changes can genuinely improve ovulation, reduce insulin resistance, and support IVF outcomes. Here is what actually works.
content.body:
PCOS is fundamentally a metabolic and hormonal condition. The dietary goal is simple: reduce insulin spikes, reduce inflammation, and support hormone balance.

Foods that help PCOS fertility:
- Low glycaemic index carbohydrates: brown rice, oats, quinoa, sweet potato (slow glucose release — reduces insulin spikes)
- High-fibre vegetables: leafy greens, broccoli, cabbage, bitter gourd
- Lean proteins: eggs, chicken, lentils, paneer, fish (improves satiety, reduces androgen effects)
- Healthy fats: nuts (especially walnuts), seeds, olive oil, avocado
- Anti-inflammatory spices: turmeric, cinnamon (shown to improve insulin sensitivity)
- Inositol-rich foods: citrus fruits, legumes, nuts (myo-inositol improves PCOS ovulation)

Foods to reduce or avoid:
- Refined carbohydrates: white rice, maida (all-purpose flour), white bread, sweets
- Sugary drinks, packaged juices, alcohol
- Trans fats: processed fried foods, biscuits, chips
- Dairy in large amounts (may worsen androgen levels in some women with PCOS)

Weight management matters enormously: losing just 5–10% of body weight restores ovulation in 60–80% of overweight women with PCOS. Dr. Ankita always pairs dietary guidance with a personalised exercise recommendation — even 30 minutes of walking 5 days a week shows measurable hormonal improvement.

Supplements evidence-supported for PCOS fertility: Myo-inositol (2g twice daily), Vitamin D (if deficient), CoQ10 (100–300mg), Omega-3 fatty acids. Always consult Dr. Ankita before starting supplements alongside fertility treatment.
content.conclusion: Small, consistent dietary changes compound powerfully over time in PCOS. Start with one change this week. At Maatritva IVF, our team provides personalised nutrition guidance alongside all fertility treatments.

title: How to Improve Egg Quality Before IVF — Proven Steps
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Practical, evidence-based steps to improve egg quality before IVF. Diet, supplements, lifestyle. Dr. Ankita Mandal, Maatritva IVF Newtown Kolkata. Start 3 months before.

content.h1: How to Improve Egg Quality Before IVF — What the Evidence Actually Says
content.intro: Egg quality is the single most important factor in IVF success. Unlike egg quantity, which is fixed, egg quality can be meaningfully influenced — particularly in the 3 months before IVF stimulation. Here is what Dr. Ankita recommends.
content.body:
The 90-day window matters because it takes approximately 90 days for an egg to mature from a resting follicle to a mature, retrievable egg. Changes made 3 months before your IVF cycle can influence the quality of eggs retrieved.

Evidence-supported strategies:

1. CoQ10 (Ubiquinol form, 400–600mg/day): Mitochondria power the egg's development and fertilisation process. CoQ10 is essential for mitochondrial function. Studies show it improves egg quality and embryo development, especially in women over 35 or with low reserve.

2. Vitamin D (2000–4000 IU/day if deficient): Vitamin D receptors are present in ovarian follicles. Deficiency is associated with lower IVF success rates. Get your level tested — aim for 40–60 ng/mL before IVF.

3. DHEA (25–75mg/day for 3 months if AMH is low): Converts to androgens and estrogens in the follicle — supports egg development. Evidence strongest for women with diminished ovarian reserve. Must be taken under medical supervision.

4. Melatonin (3mg at night): Acts as a powerful antioxidant in the follicular fluid. May protect eggs from oxidative damage during stimulation. Some fertility units use it routinely.

5. Anti-inflammatory diet: Reduce processed foods, sugar, refined carbs. Increase colourful vegetables, berries, oily fish, nuts, and olive oil. Inflammation directly impairs egg cell DNA integrity.

6. Quit smoking immediately: Smoking accelerates ovarian aging by up to 10 years and damages mtDNA in eggs. There is no safe level of smoking for fertility.

7. Limit alcohol: Even 1–2 units daily has been shown to reduce IVF pregnancy rates by 20%.

8. Stress management: Cortisol impairs the hormonal cascade that triggers ovulation. Yoga, mindfulness meditation, and regular sleep schedules have measurable hormonal benefits.
content.conclusion: Three months of intentional preparation can genuinely shift your IVF outcome. Dr. Ankita provides every patient with a personalised pre-IVF optimisation plan at Maatritva IVF, Newtown Kolkata.

title: How to Improve Sperm Count Naturally — 10 Proven Methods
author: Dr. Chhabi Ghosh
metaDescription: Proven ways to improve sperm count and motility naturally. Dr. Chhabi Ghosh at Maatritva IVF Kolkata shares the most effective lifestyle and supplement strategies backed by evidence.

content.h1: How to Improve Sperm Count Naturally — 10 Evidence-Based Methods
content.intro: Male fertility is directly reversible by lifestyle in many cases — because sperm are completely renewed every 72–90 days. What you do in the next 3 months directly shapes the sperm that will be used in treatment.
content.body:
1. Quit smoking: Smoking reduces sperm count by 23% and motility by 13% on average. DNA fragmentation in smokers' sperm is significantly elevated. This is the single most impactful change any man can make.

2. Limit alcohol: More than 5 units per week impairs testosterone production and sperm quality. Aim for fewer than 3 units per week during the preconception period.

3. Maintain healthy weight: Both underweight and overweight men show impaired sperm quality. Obesity raises scrotal temperature and converts testosterone to estrogen via fat cell aromatase activity.

4. Avoid heat exposure: Sperm production requires temperatures 2–3°C below core body temperature. Avoid prolonged hot baths, saunas, hot tub use, and laptops directly on the lap. Loose-fitting underwear helps.

5. Take antioxidant supplements: Oxidative stress damages sperm DNA. Evidence-supported supplements: Zinc (25mg), Selenium (100mcg), Vitamin C (1000mg), Vitamin E (400IU), CoQ10 (200–400mg), L-carnitine (2g/day). Always check with Dr. Chhabi Ghosh before starting.

6. Manage stress: Chronic psychological stress elevates cortisol, which suppresses testosterone. Regular exercise, adequate sleep (7–8 hours), and mindfulness measurably improve testosterone levels.

7. Exercise moderately: Regular aerobic exercise improves testosterone and sperm quality. Avoid excessive endurance training or steroid use — these suppress sperm production.

8. Check medications: Several common medications reduce sperm production, including testosterone supplements, anabolic steroids, some antidepressants (SSRIs), calcium channel blockers, and sulfasalazine. Discuss with Dr. Ghosh before stopping any medication.

9. Get a varicocele assessment: Dilated scrotal veins raise testicular temperature and directly impair sperm. Treatment can significantly improve parameters.

10. Get tested — do not guess: A full semen analysis with DNA fragmentation gives precise information. Many men find their lifestyle interventions improve parameters to the point where IVF or ICSI is no longer needed.
content.conclusion: Three months of focused effort can produce a measurably different semen analysis. Book a semen analysis at Maatritva IVF, Newtown Kolkata and let Dr. Chhabi Ghosh review your results personally.

title: Sperm DNA Fragmentation — The Hidden Cause of IVF Failure
author: Dr. Chhabi Ghosh
metaDescription: Sperm DNA fragmentation (DFI) explained simply. How it causes IVF failure and miscarriage, and how to treat it. Dr. Chhabi Ghosh, Maatritva IVF Newtown Kolkata.

content.h1: Sperm DNA Fragmentation — The Hidden Cause of Unexplained IVF Failure
content.intro: Your IVF failed. Semen analysis is 'normal.' The embryo looked perfect on Day 5. So why no pregnancy? Sperm DNA fragmentation could be the answer no one has checked yet.
content.body:
What is sperm DNA fragmentation?
DNA fragmentation index (DFI) measures whether the genetic material inside sperm is damaged or broken (fragmented). Sperm may look completely normal under a microscope and swim perfectly well — yet carry significant DNA damage that prevents healthy embryo development.

Why does it matter?
High DFI (above 25%) is strongly associated with:
- Reduced IVF and ICSI fertilisation rates
- Poorer embryo quality and higher fragmentation
- Recurrent implantation failure (embryos not sticking)
- Recurrent miscarriage (even with good-looking embryos)

Causes of high DFI:
- Smoking (single biggest cause)
- Heat exposure (saunas, hot baths, fever)
- Oxidative stress from poor diet and sedentary lifestyle
- Varicocele (most common clinical cause)
- Infections (prostatitis, epididymitis)
- Age (DFI increases with age)
- Chemotherapy or radiation

How is it treated?
- Address root cause — treat varicocele, quit smoking, antioxidants, avoid heat
- ICSI with MACS (magnetic activated cell sorting) or PICSI (selecting sperm by hyaluronate binding) selects lower-DFI sperm
- Surgical sperm retrieval (TESA) — sperm from the testes have lower DFI than ejaculated sperm in high-DFI cases
- Repeat testing after 3 months of lifestyle intervention

At Maatritva IVF, DFI testing is recommended for all couples with unexplained IVF failure, recurrent miscarriage, or poor embryo quality despite good semen analysis.
content.conclusion: If your IVF has failed with no clear reason, DFI testing is one of the most important next steps. Book a male fertility evaluation at Maatritva IVF, Newtown Kolkata.

title: IUI vs IVF — Which Should You Choose First?
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: IUI vs IVF — how do you decide which to try first? Dr. Ankita Mandal at Maatritva IVF Kolkata explains the decision framework clearly and compassionately.

content.h1: IUI vs IVF — How to Decide Which to Try First
content.intro: IUI or IVF first? It is one of the most common questions at Maatritva IVF. The answer is never one-size-fits-all — but there is a clear, evidence-based framework Dr. Ankita uses to guide every couple.
content.body:
IUI is appropriate when:
- Both fallopian tubes are open
- Sperm count and motility are mild-to-moderately reduced (count >5 million motile)
- Ovulation can be stimulated or timed effectively
- The woman is under 35 with good ovarian reserve
- The diagnosis is unexplained infertility and you have time to try this gentler step
- Cost is a significant consideration (IUI costs ₹8,000–₹20,000 vs ₹1.2L–₹2.5L for IVF)

IVF is recommended directly when:
- Both fallopian tubes are blocked
- Severe male factor infertility (requires ICSI)
- Female age is 38 or older
- Failed 3–4 IUI cycles
- Advanced endometriosis (Stage III–IV)
- Very low AMH or poor ovarian reserve
- PGT (genetic testing of embryos) is needed

The important comparison:
- IUI success rate: 15–22% per cycle
- IVF success rate: 55–70% per cycle (under 35)

Skipping IUI to go straight to IVF is sometimes the right decision — especially for older women where time is critical. Spending 4–6 months on IUI cycles that have little chance of success can mean a critical reduction in IVF success due to age.

Dr. Ankita discusses this framework openly with every couple. She considers your specific diagnosis, age, ovarian reserve, sperm quality, budget, and emotional readiness before recommending a path.
content.conclusion: There is no universally right answer — but there IS a right answer for your specific situation. Book a consultation at Maatritva IVF, Newtown Kolkata and let Dr. Ankita map your personal fertility roadmap.

title: Why Does IVF Fail? The 7 Most Common Reasons
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Why does IVF fail? Dr. Ankita Mandal at Maatritva IVF Kolkata explains the 7 most common reasons for IVF failure and what can be done differently next cycle.

content.h1: Why Does IVF Fail? The 7 Most Common Reasons — Explained by Dr. Ankita Mandal
content.intro: A failed IVF cycle is emotionally devastating. But understanding why it failed — specifically, not generically — is the most important step toward a successful next attempt. Here are the seven most common reasons.
content.body:
1. Embryo chromosomal abnormality (most common)
Up to 50–70% of all embryos — even those that look perfect on Day 5 — carry chromosomal errors that prevent implantation or cause early miscarriage. This is the leading cause of IVF failure, especially in women over 35. Solution: PGT-A testing selects only chromosomally normal embryos for transfer.

2. Poor egg quality
Related to age, AMH, and oxidative stress. Even good-looking embryos may have compromised mitochondrial function. Solution: Pre-IVF optimisation (CoQ10, DHEA, antioxidants) + personalised stimulation protocol.

3. Poor sperm DNA quality
High DNA fragmentation in sperm causes early embryo arrest even after fertilisation. Solution: DFI testing, ICSI with sperm selection techniques (PICSI/MACS), or TESA.

4. Uterine receptivity issues
A cavity with polyps, fibroids, adhesions, or thin endometrium will not accept even the best embryo. Solution: Hysteroscopy, ERA test (endometrial receptivity assay) to find the optimal implantation window.

5. Stimulation protocol mismatch
Over-stimulation or under-stimulation affects egg quality. The wrong protocol for your AMH, age, or diagnosis is a preventable cause. Solution: Protocol adjustment based on your specific response and reserve assessment.

6. Implantation failure (displaced window)
The endometrium is most receptive for only a narrow 12–24 hour window each cycle. The ERA test identifies if your window is shifted — and allows transfer timing to be personalised.

7. Lifestyle factors
Smoking, high BMI, alcohol, uncontrolled thyroid or blood sugar, and unaddressed stress all reduce IVF success rates. These are modifiable — and should be addressed before the next cycle.
content.conclusion: A failed IVF cycle is information, not a dead end. At Maatritva IVF, Dr. Ankita conducts a thorough cycle review after every failure and creates a clearly reasoned plan for what to do differently next time.

title: HSG Test — What It Is, What to Expect, and What Results Mean
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: HSG test for blocked tubes explained simply. What is an HSG, does it hurt, what do results mean? Dr. Ankita Mandal, Maatritva IVF Newtown Kolkata.

content.h1: HSG Test for Blocked Tubes — What to Expect, Explained Simply
content.intro: Your doctor has recommended an HSG test. You have Googled it and you are nervous. This guide tells you exactly what happens, whether it hurts, and what your results mean — from a doctor who performs them regularly.
content.body:
What is an HSG?
HSG (Hysterosalpingography) is an outpatient X-ray procedure where a water-soluble dye is injected through the cervix into the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes. The dye shows up on X-ray and reveals the shape of the uterine cavity and whether both tubes are open, blocked, or damaged.

When is it recommended?
For any woman with infertility, especially when PID, endometriosis, previous ectopic pregnancy, or pelvic infection is suspected.

When is it done?
Days 7–10 of your menstrual cycle — after menstruation ends but before ovulation. This minimises the risk of accidental radiation exposure to a newly fertilised egg.

Does it hurt?
Most women describe it as cramps similar to or slightly stronger than period pains — lasting 10–15 minutes during and after the dye injection. Taking an NSAID (ibuprofen) 1 hour before the test significantly reduces discomfort. You can return to normal activities the same day.

What do results mean?
Normal result: Dye flows freely through both tubes and spills into the pelvis — both tubes are open.

Abnormal results: Dye stops midway (blocked tube), fills only part of the cavity (fibroid or polyp), or shows an irregular shape (septum or adhesions).

Important note: HSG has a false positive rate for tubal blockage — muscle spasm during the test can mimic a block. Laparoscopy is the gold standard for confirming true blockage.

The 'therapeutic effect' of HSG: Studies show conception rates improve in the 3–6 months after HSG, possibly because the dye flushes mild mucus or debris. This is modest but real.
content.conclusion: If you need an HSG, Dr. Ankita at Maatritva IVF will perform it gently, review the results immediately, and explain your next steps. Book today.

title: Azoospermia Explained — Zero Sperm: Causes, Types and Options
author: Dr. Chhabi Ghosh
metaDescription: Azoospermia (zero sperm count) explained simply. Causes, obstructive vs non-obstructive, treatment options. Dr. Chhabi Ghosh, Maatritva IVF Newtown Kolkata.

content.h1: Azoospermia Explained — Zero Sperm in the Ejaculate: What It Means and What You Can Do
content.intro: A result showing zero sperm in an ejaculate sample — azoospermia — is not a sentence. It is a starting point for investigation. Dr. Chhabi Ghosh explains everything you need to know.
content.body:
Azoospermia affects approximately 1 in 100 men and about 10–15% of all infertile men. There are two types — and the type determines the treatment.

Type 1: Obstructive Azoospermia (OA)
Sperm are being produced normally in the testes but cannot exit due to a blockage — in the epididymis, vas deferens, or ejaculatory ducts.

Causes: Vasectomy, previous epididymal infection, congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (CBAVD, linked to CFTR gene), prior hernia surgery that accidentally damaged the vas.

Sperm retrieval success: Very high (>90%) with PESA or TESA. Quality of retrieved sperm is excellent.

Type 2: Non-Obstructive Azoospermia (NOA)
The testes are not producing enough sperm — due to testicular failure, hormonal disruption, or genetic abnormality.

Causes: Klinefelter syndrome (47XXY), Y-chromosome microdeletions, Sertoli cell only syndrome, previous chemotherapy, mumps orchitis, undescended testes.

Sperm retrieval: Possible in 40–60% of NOA cases via micro-TESE — a microsurgical technique that searches the testicle for small pockets of active sperm production.

How is it diagnosed?
Repeat semen analysis (confirm) → FSH/LH/testosterone levels → Karyotype + Y-microdeletion → Testicular ultrasound → Testicular biopsy in selected cases.

FSH interpretation:
- Low/normal FSH = likely obstructive (good prognosis)
- High FSH = testicular impairment (non-obstructive; prognosis variable)

What if no sperm are found?
Donor sperm via IUI or IVF remains an option — allowing the female partner to be the biological mother. Dr. Chhabi Ghosh discusses all options with complete transparency and compassion.
content.conclusion: Azoospermia is not the end of the road. Let Dr. Chhabi Ghosh evaluate your case at Maatritva IVF, Newtown Kolkata and map every available option.

title: Best Age to Freeze Eggs — When Is the Right Time?
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: When is the best age to freeze eggs? Dr. Ankita Mandal at Maatritva IVF Kolkata explains the optimal window, what to expect, and whether egg freezing is right for you.

content.h1: Best Age to Freeze Eggs — When Should You Act?
content.intro: Egg freezing is a decision women are making younger and younger — for career, life circumstances, or simply because they want options. As someone who guides women through this decision regularly, Dr. Ankita Mandal gives you the honest answer.
content.body:
The optimal window for egg freezing is age 28–34.

Why?
- Egg quantity is still good (AMH typically 1.5–4.0 ng/mL)
- Egg quality is near peak
- More eggs retrieved per cycle = better future success odds
- Fewer injections needed compared to older age
- Greater number of cycles remaining for use

Age 35–37: Still a good time to freeze, but expect fewer eggs and slightly lower quality. May need 2 cycles to achieve 15–20 mature eggs stored.

Age 38–40: Can still attempt, but significantly fewer eggs retrieved per cycle and quality declines. Multiple cycles often needed. Discuss with Dr. Ankita whether own-egg freezing or donor eggs make more sense given your specific AMH.

Age 40+: Own-egg freezing becomes progressively less effective. Discuss realistic outcomes honestly with Dr. Ankita.

How many eggs do I need?
The standard guidance is 15–20 mature frozen eggs to give a reasonably good chance of one live birth in the future. Each egg has approximately a 5–7% chance of resulting in a live birth when used at age 35–38. More stored eggs = more attempts = better cumulative odds.

Is egg freezing 100% guaranteed?
No. Eggs can be damaged during freezing/thawing, fail to fertilise, or produce embryos that do not implant. This is why freezing earlier, when more and better-quality eggs are available, significantly improves future odds.

Cost in Kolkata: ₹80,000–₹1,50,000 for the retrieval cycle and first year of storage. Annual storage fees apply thereafter.
content.conclusion: The best time to freeze eggs was yesterday. The second best time is today. Book a fertility assessment with Dr. Ankita Mandal at Maatritva IVF, Newtown Kolkata.

title: Thyroid and Pregnancy — Everything You Must Know
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Thyroid and pregnancy guide from Dr. Ankita Mandal at Maatritva IVF Kolkata. Hypothyroidism, TSH targets, medication dosing, and why thyroid testing is mandatory before IVF.

content.h1: Thyroid and Pregnancy — Everything You Must Know Before Conceiving
content.intro: Thyroid disorders affect up to 1 in 5 women in India — and yet thyroid testing before pregnancy or IVF is still not routine everywhere. Dr. Ankita Mandal explains why it absolutely should be.
content.body:
Why the thyroid matters so much for pregnancy:
The thyroid produces T3 and T4 hormones that regulate metabolism — but in pregnancy, these hormones are also critical for fetal brain development, placental formation, and maintaining the uterine lining.

Hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid):
- Causes irregular or absent ovulation
- Increases miscarriage risk by 2–3x
- Impairs embryo implantation
- Can affect fetal neurological development if untreated in early pregnancy
- Even subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 2.5–4.0) in women trying to conceive is associated with poorer outcomes

Target TSH for conception and early pregnancy:
- Trying to conceive: TSH < 2.5 mIU/L
- First trimester: TSH < 2.5 mIU/L
- Second trimester: TSH < 3.0 mIU/L
- Third trimester: TSH < 3.5 mIU/L
- These are stricter than the general population normal range (0.5–4.5)

Hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid):
- Causes irregular periods and early pregnancy loss
- Requires treatment before conception (antithyroid medication, dose adjusted carefully)
- Graves' disease antibodies can cross the placenta — requires monitoring

Hashimoto's thyroiditis:
- Autoimmune condition causing hypothyroidism
- TPO antibodies associated with higher miscarriage rate even when TSH is normal
- Dr. Ankita monitors TPO-positive patients closely regardless of TSH value

Dose adjustment in pregnancy:
- Most women on levothyroxine need a 25–30% dose increase by Week 6–8 of pregnancy
- TSH must be rechecked every 4–6 weeks in first trimester
- Missing doses in early pregnancy has real consequences — do not skip
content.conclusion: Every woman at Maatritva IVF has her TSH checked at the first consultation — it is non-negotiable. If you are trying to conceive anywhere in Kolkata and have not had this test, book with us today.

title: PGT-A Explained — Should You Test Your Embryos Before Transfer?
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: PGT-A preimplantation genetic testing explained. Who needs it, how it works, and whether it improves IVF success. Dr. Ankita Mandal, Maatritva IVF Newtown Kolkata.

content.h1: PGT-A Explained — Should You Test Your Embryos Genetically Before Transfer?
content.intro: PGT-A is one of the most discussed — and most misunderstood — advances in IVF. Here is what it actually does, who genuinely benefits, and when it may not be necessary.
content.body:
What is PGT-A?
Preimplantation Genetic Testing for Aneuploidies (PGT-A) involves biopsy of a few cells from a Day 5 blastocyst embryo, followed by chromosomal analysis in a genetic lab. It identifies whether the embryo has the correct number of chromosomes (46, XX or 46, XY = normal/euploid) versus chromosomal errors (aneuploidies such as Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, etc.).

Only euploid (chromosomally normal) embryos are transferred.

Who genuinely benefits from PGT-A:
- Women aged 37 or older (higher rate of chromosomal errors per embryo)
- Couples with recurrent IVF failure (2+ failed transfers with good-looking embryos)
- Recurrent miscarriage where embryo genetics are suspected
- Couples who produce many blastocysts and want to identify the best one
- Severe male factor infertility (higher sperm DNA fragmentation increases aneuploidy risk)

Who may NOT need PGT-A:
- Women under 35 with good prognosis and limited embryos (testing may reduce usable transfers if embryos are mosaic or have biopsy damage)
- Couples with only 1–2 blastocysts (testing is expensive; it may leave no transfers if the one embryo is abnormal)

Limitations and honest caveats:
- Mosaic embryos (both normal and abnormal cells) are increasingly considered potentially viable
- PGT-A does not test for all genetic disorders — only chromosomal number
- Biopsied embryos must be frozen (no fresh transfer) adding cost and one cycle of waiting
- Cost: Adds ₹40,000–₹80,000 to an IVF cycle

Dr. Ankita's approach: PGT-A is recommended selectively — not as a blanket add-on. She discusses the genuine cost-benefit analysis transparently with each patient before suggesting it.
content.conclusion: PGT-A can be genuinely transformative for the right patients — and unnecessary for others. Book a consultation at Maatritva IVF to discuss whether it is right for your specific situation.

title: Pregnancy After IVF — What to Expect and How to Manage It
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Pregnant after IVF? Dr. Ankita Mandal at Maatritva IVF Kolkata guides you through the first trimester, medication tapering, and managing anxiety after a hard fertility journey.

content.h1: Pregnant After IVF — What Actually Happens Next and How to Navigate It
content.intro: You have just seen the positive beta-hCG result. After everything you have been through, this is the moment. But IVF pregnancy can come with unique questions and anxieties. Here is what to expect.
content.body:
The first 48–72 hours: Repeat beta-hCG
A single positive beta-hCG is not enough — we always repeat the test 48–72 hours later. The level should roughly double in this time. A rising beta confirms a developing pregnancy. Levels that plateau or fall may indicate a chemical pregnancy or early loss — devastating but important to know quickly.

Week 5–6: First ultrasound
We look for the gestational sac and, by 6 weeks, a fetal heartbeat. This first heartbeat scan after IVF is one of the most emotional moments for our patients — and for us.

Continuing medications:
Most IVF pregnancies require progesterone supplementation (pessaries or injections) until 10–12 weeks of pregnancy. Do not stop without Dr. Ankita's guidance — the placenta takes over progesterone production gradually. Stopping too early risks early pregnancy loss.

After the first trimester:
- Most IVF pregnancies following this are managed like any other pregnancy
- Twin pregnancies (more common with IVF) require closer monitoring throughout
- Women with underlying conditions (PCOS, thyroid, fibroids) need ongoing surveillance

Handling anxiety:
Postpartum anxiety and hypervigilance about baby movements, spotting, and symptoms are extremely common after a difficult fertility journey. This is normal and valid. Dr. Ankita's team provides emotional support alongside medical monitoring.

When symptoms are concerning:
- Significant bleeding (more than spotting) — call us immediately
- Severe abdominal pain
- Fever above 38°C
- No fetal heartbeat on a scheduled scan

For most routine concerns (light spotting, mild cramping, nausea), reassurance and an extra scan is usually all that is needed.
content.conclusion: After working so hard for this pregnancy, you deserve to enjoy it with the right support. Our team at Maatritva IVF in Newtown remains with you through every step — from positive beta-hCG to delivery.

title: Fertility Preservation Before Cancer Treatment — A Complete Guide
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Fertility preservation before chemotherapy or radiation. Egg, embryo and sperm freezing. Urgent timeline. Dr. Ankita Mandal, Maatritva IVF Newtown Kolkata. Start within days.

content.h1: Fertility Preservation Before Cancer Treatment — Your Complete Guide
content.intro: A cancer diagnosis changes everything. Fertility preservation gives you back one choice — the choice to have children when you are ready. Dr. Ankita Mandal explains what is possible, how quickly it can be done, and what to expect.
content.body:
Why cancer treatment threatens fertility:
Chemotherapy (particularly alkylating agents: cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) and pelvic radiation damage rapidly dividing cells — including the eggs in the ovaries and the sperm-producing cells in the testes. The extent of damage depends on the drug type, dose, and whether the pelvis is in the radiation field.

How quickly do we need to act?
For women: Egg or embryo freezing requires 10–14 days of ovarian stimulation before egg retrieval. Using random-start protocols, we can begin on any day of the menstrual cycle — no waiting for a specific timing. We coordinate urgently with your oncologist to fit within the pre-treatment window.

For men: Sperm freezing requires only a single visit — 2–3 samples collected over several days. This should be done before any chemotherapy begins, even one cycle. Sperm banking takes under 2 hours.

Options for women:
- Egg freezing: Mature eggs frozen after stimulation and retrieval
- Embryo freezing: Eggs fertilised with partner or donor sperm before freezing (slightly higher per-embryo survival)
- Ovarian tissue freezing: Experimental in India; available in select centres for girls/women who cannot delay treatment
- GnRH agonist co-treatment: Medications given alongside chemo to 'switch off' the ovaries temporarily; evidence is supportive but not conclusive

Funding and support:
MAatritva IVF works sensitively with patients in financial difficulty. Some insurance plans cover fertility preservation for cancer patients — always ask your insurers.
content.conclusion: Do not wait until after treatment to think about fertility. Act now. Call Maatritva IVF on +91 8100 343839 and we will coordinate an urgent consultation within 24–48 hours.

title: Age and IVF Success — The Honest Truth
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: How does age genuinely affect IVF success? Dr. Ankita Mandal at Maatritva IVF Kolkata explains egg quality decline, when to consider donor eggs, and the importance of not waiting.

content.h1: Age and IVF Success — The Biology, The Numbers, and What It Means for You
content.intro: Fertility declines with age — that is biology, not opinion. But the decline is not a cliff edge. It is a slope with different gradients at different ages. Here is what you actually need to know.
content.body:
The core biology:
Women are born with all the eggs they will ever have (approximately 1–2 million at birth). By puberty, this falls to 400,000. By 37, it typically falls below 25,000 — and accelerates from there. More importantly with age, the proportion of chromosomally abnormal eggs increases dramatically:

- Age 30: ~20% of eggs are chromosomally abnormal
- Age 35: ~40% abnormal
- Age 40: ~60–70% abnormal
- Age 43+: ~80–90% abnormal

This is why IVF success rates fall with age — multiple embryos are created, but fewer are chromosomally viable.

With PGT-A (genetic embryo testing):
Success per transfer is improved because only normal embryos are transferred. However, PGT-A cannot create more normal embryos — it only identifies which of the ones you have are viable. If reserve is low, there may be fewer embryos to test.

The 'wait and see' risk:
Delay at 35 becomes urgency at 38. A woman who waits 2 years will typically retrieve significantly fewer eggs and have lower success rates. This is the most common regret Dr. Ankita hears from late-30s patients: 'I wish I had come sooner.'

When donor eggs become the right conversation:
- Age 43+ with own eggs
- AMH < 0.3 at any age
- 2–3 failed IVF cycles with poor response
- When the evidence clearly shows own-egg chances are too low to justify the emotional and financial cost

Dr. Ankita approaches this conversation with compassion and absolute transparency — never pressure.
content.conclusion: If you are in your mid-to-late 30s and thinking about children, the most valuable thing you can do is get a fertility assessment now. It is free of obligation and full of information.

title: Should You Have Surgery Before IVF? — A Doctor's Guide
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Should you have laparoscopy or hysteroscopy before IVF? Dr. Ankita Mandal at Maatritva IVF Kolkata explains when surgery improves IVF outcomes and when it is unnecessary.

content.h1: Should You Have Surgery Before IVF? Your Gynaecologist's Honest Guide
content.intro: Surgery before IVF is sometimes essential — and sometimes unnecessary. Dr. Ankita Mandal walks you through the specific conditions where surgery significantly improves IVF success, and those where going straight to IVF is the right call.
content.body:
Cases where surgery BEFORE IVF is strongly recommended:

1. Hydrosalpinx (fluid-filled blocked tube): The fluid from a hydrosalpinx is toxic to embryos and leaks into the uterine cavity. Studies show hydrosalpinx reduces IVF success by up to 50%. Removing the affected tube (salpingectomy) before IVF is strongly evidence-supported.

2. Submucosal fibroids: Even small fibroids inside the uterine cavity significantly reduce implantation rates. Hysteroscopic removal before IVF is recommended.

3. Uterine polyps: Multiple studies confirm polyp removal before IVF improves implantation rates by 30–50%. This is a simple day procedure.

4. Uterine septum: A partial or complete septum dividing the uterine cavity is associated with recurrent miscarriage and implantation failure. Hysteroscopic septoplasty corrects this before IVF.

5. Severe endometriosis (Stage III–IV): Management is nuanced. For large endometriomas (>4cm), surgery may be appropriate. For bilateral endometriomas, protecting ovarian reserve during surgery is critical.

Cases where going DIRECTLY to IVF is usually the right call:
- Bilateral tubal blockage without hydrosalpinx: IVF bypasses tubes entirely — surgery rarely adds value
- Small intramural fibroids not distorting the cavity: IVF without surgery first is appropriate
- Mild endometriosis (Stage I–II): IVF directly may be recommended especially in older patients where time matters
content.conclusion: The 'right' surgery decision is individualised. At Maatritva IVF, Dr. Ankita reviews your scans and history before recommending surgery — never reflexively.

title: Gestational Diabetes — Managing It for a Healthy Pregnancy
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Gestational diabetes management in pregnancy. Diet, monitoring, medication, and delivery planning. Dr. Ankita Mandal, Maatritva IVF Newtown Kolkata. Expert high-risk care.

content.h1: Gestational Diabetes in Pregnancy — How to Manage It and Keep Your Baby Safe
content.intro: Gestational diabetes (GDM) is diagnosed in up to 1 in 7 Indian pregnancies — higher than global averages due to genetic predisposition. The good news: with the right management, most women with GDM have completely healthy pregnancies and babies.
content.body:
What is gestational diabetes?
GDM is a form of glucose intolerance that first develops during pregnancy. It occurs when pregnancy hormones (particularly human placental lactogen) cause insulin resistance — meaning your body cannot produce enough insulin to maintain normal blood sugar levels.

When is it screened?
At Maatritva IVF, all pregnant patients undergo a glucose challenge test (GCT) at 24–28 weeks. High-risk patients (PCOS, family history, obesity, previous GDM) are screened earlier.

Risks of uncontrolled GDM:
- Baby: Macrosomia (large baby), difficult delivery, neonatal hypoglycaemia, increased risk of childhood obesity and diabetes
- Mother: Pre-eclampsia, increased C-section risk, future risk of Type 2 diabetes

Management approach:
Step 1 — Diet: Low glycaemic index eating (same principles as PCOS diet). Spread carbohydrates evenly across 6 small meals. Avoid all sugary drinks, white rice in large quantities, sweets.

Step 2 — Blood sugar monitoring: Self-testing before meals and 1 hour after meals. Fasting target: <95 mg/dL; 1-hour post-meal: <140 mg/dL.

Step 3 — Medication: If diet alone does not control levels within 1–2 weeks, insulin is added. Insulin in GDM is completely safe for the baby. Do not delay this step if diet is insufficient.

Step 4 — Delivery planning: Discuss timing at 36 weeks. Induction at 38–39 weeks is usually recommended if macrosomia or blood sugar control is difficult. C-section planned if baby position or size warrants it.
content.conclusion: Gestational diabetes is manageable — and the Maatritva IVF team provides hands-on dietary coaching, blood sugar review, and delivery planning for all affected patients.

title: Managing Endometriosis Pain — Practical Strategies That Work
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Endometriosis pain management strategies from Dr. Ankita Mandal at Maatritva IVF Kolkata. Medical, surgical, and lifestyle approaches that genuinely reduce pain.

content.h1: Managing Endometriosis Pain — Strategies That Actually Work
content.intro: Endometriosis pain is real, often severe, and frequently dismissed. You do not have to just 'live with it.' Dr. Ankita Mandal shares medical, surgical, and lifestyle approaches that can genuinely reduce endometriosis pain.
content.body:
Understanding the pain:
Endometriosis pain comes from inflammatory chemicals released by ectopic endometrial tissue, adhesions that pull on organs during movement, and nerve sensitisation caused by years of uncontrolled inflammation.

Medical management (non-hormonal):
- NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen): Start 1–2 days before expected period pain. Most effective when taken continuously through the painful episode, not just when pain peaks.
- Antispasmodics: For bowel-related endometriosis pain

Hormonal management (for non-fertility contexts):
- Combined oral contraceptive pill: Continuously (no pill-free week) reduces monthly bleeds and ectopic bleeding
- Progestin-only therapy: Norethisterone, dienogest — effective for moderate-to-severe pain
- GnRH agonists (Leuprolide): Temporary 'medical menopause' — very effective for severe pain but cause significant side effects; not suitable for long-term use
- Mirena IUS: Intrauterine progesterone reduces pain particularly for deep infiltrating endometriosis

Surgical management:
- Laparoscopic excision (not just fulguration) is the gold standard — removes endometriotic tissue at the root
- Recurrence rates are lower with excision than ablation
- Not always appropriate before IVF if ovarian reserve is at risk

Lifestyle strategies that help:
- Anti-inflammatory diet (omega-3, turmeric, avoid red meat)
- Regular moderate exercise (reduces prostaglandin-driven pain)
- Heat therapy (heated pad on abdomen during pain)
- Magnesium supplementation (400mg/day — reduces uterine cramping)
- Stress management — cortisol worsens inflammation
content.conclusion: Endometriosis pain should be taken seriously and managed proactively. Dr. Ankita at Maatritva IVF treats the condition and the pain — not just your fertility goals.

title: What is an AMH Test? Understanding Anti-Mullerian Hormone
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: What is an AMH test and what do the results mean for your fertility? Dr. Ankita Mandal explains normal levels, testing, and what low AMH means in Kolkata.

content.h1: What is an AMH Test? Understanding Your Fertility Potential
content.intro: The Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) test is one of the most important fertility tests available today. But what exactly does it measure, and more importantly, what does your result mean for your chances of having a baby? Dr. Ankita Mandal explains.
content.body:
What does AMH measure?
AMH is a hormone produced by the small, growing follicles (sac-like structures containing premature eggs) in your ovaries. Because it remains relatively stable throughout your menstrual cycle, an AMH blood test is a reliable indicator of your 'ovarian reserve' — an estimate of how many eggs you currently have left.

Important: AMH measures egg QUANTITY, not egg QUALITY. A low AMH does not mean you cannot conceive, and a high AMH does not guarantee pregnancy.

What are normal AMH levels?
While 'normal' varies slightly by age, general guidelines are:
- High ( souvent seen in PCOS): Over 4.0 ng/mL
- Normal/Good: 1.5 - 4.0 ng/mL
- Low-Normal: 1.0 - 1.5 ng/mL
- Low: Under 1.0 ng/mL
- Very Low: Under 0.5 ng/mL

When should you get an AMH test?
- If you have been trying to conceive for 6+ months and are over 35
- If you are considering egg freezing
- If you have a family history of early menopause
- Before starting any fertility treatment (IUI or IVF)
- If you have had previous ovarian surgery (e.g., for endometriosis)

What if your AMH is low?
A low AMH level is not a reason to panic, but it is a reason to act. It indicates that you have a smaller window of time. If you are trying to conceive naturally, it may take longer. If you are doing IVF, it means you may end up with fewer eggs retrieved during a cycle, and you might need modified stimulation protocols or multiple cycles. Dr. Ankita specialises in tailoring protocols specifically for low AMH patients.

Can you improve your AMH?
AMH naturally declines with age and cannot be permanently increased. However, supplements like DHEA and Vitamin D (if deficient) can sometimes help optimise the function of the remaining follicles before IVF.
content.conclusion: Your AMH is a piece of information, not a final verdict. If you are concerned about your ovarian reserve, book a consultation at Maatritva IVF in Newtown to discuss a proactive plan.

title: Early Signs of Pregnancy After IVF Transfer
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: The two-week wait after IVF transfer is stressful. Learn the real early signs of pregnancy and what symptoms are just from medication. Dr. Ankita Mandal, Maatritva IVF.

content.h1: Early Signs of Pregnancy After IVF Transfer — What to Look For
content.intro: The 'two-week wait' between embryo transfer and the pregnancy test is often the most anxiety-inducing part of IVF. You analyse every twinge. But what are the real signs of pregnancy, and what is just a side effect of medication?
content.body:
The truth about symptoms:
The most important thing to know is that many early pregnancy symptoms are identical to the side effects of the progesterone and estrogen you are taking for the IVF cycle. Having symptoms does not strictly guarantee pregnancy, and having NO symptoms does not mean the cycle failed.

Common signs (which could be pregnancy OR medication):

1. Spotting or light bleeding: Often called 'implantation bleeding', this can occur 5-7 days after transfer. It is usually light pink or brown and very brief. However, spotting can also just be a side effect of progesterone suppositories or the transfer procedure itself.

2. Cramping: Mild cramping is very common as the uterus prepares for implantation, but also common from progesterone. Severe cramping should be reported to your doctor.

3. Breast tenderness: Swollen, heavy, or tender breasts are classic early pregnancy signs, but also very common from hormone medications.

4. Fatigue: Profound tiredness is a hallmark of early pregnancy (due to rising progesterone levels), but again, you are taking supplemental progesterone.

5. Nausea: True 'morning sickness' usually starts closer to 6 weeks, but some women report mild nausea or food aversions earlier.

6. Frequent urination: Hormonal changes and increased blood volume can make you need the bathroom more often.

7. Missed period: If you are taking progesterone, it will usually prevent your period from starting, regardless of whether you are pregnant.

When to test:
We strongly advise waiting for the scheduled beta-hCG blood test (usually 10-14 days post-transfer). Home urine tests can give false positives (from an HCG trigger shot) or false negatives (if tested too early).

When to contact the clinic immediately:
- Heavy bleeding (like a strong period)
- Severe abdominal or pelvic pain
- Fever or flu-like symptoms
content.conclusion: The two-week wait is hard. Try to find healthy distractions and lean on your support system. At Maatritva IVF, our team is always just a phone call away to answer your questions during this time.

title: Understanding PCOS: Beyond Just Irregular Periods
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: PCOS is more than just irregular periods. Learn about the hidden symptoms, insulin resistance, and how it really affects fertility. Dr. Ankita Mandal, Maatritva IVF.

content.h1: Understanding PCOS: It Is More Than Just Irregular Periods
content.intro: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is incredibly common, affecting up to 1 in 5 women of reproductive age in India. Most women associate it with missed periods, but PCOS is a complex metabolic and endocrine disorder that affects the whole body.
content.body:
The Core Features of PCOS:
A diagnosis of PCOS typically requires two of the following three criteria (the Rotterdam criteria):
1. Irregular or absent periods (oligo/anovulation)
2. Signs of high androgens (male hormones) — such as excess facial/body hair, acne, or male-pattern hair loss
3. Polycystic ovaries seen on ultrasound (multiple small follicles, giving a 'pearl necklace' appearance)

The Hidden Symptoms:
Beyond the diagnostic criteria, many women with PCOS struggle with symptoms that impact their daily lives:
- Weight gain or severe difficulty losing weight
- Fatigue and low energy
- Skin tags or dark patches of skin (acanthosis nigricans), especially on the neck or armpits (signs of insulin resistance)
- Mood changes, depression, and anxiety
- Sleep apnea

The Role of Insulin Resistance:
Up to 70-80% of women with PCOS have insulin resistance, meaning their bodies produce insulin but cannot use it effectively. To compensate, the pancreas pumps out more insulin. High insulin levels trigger the ovaries to produce more androgens (testosterone), which then disrupts ovulation and worsens symptoms like weight gain and hair growth. This creates a vicious cycle.

How PCOS Affects Fertility:
The primary fertility issue is anovulation. Since you are not releasing an egg every month (or at all), conception naturally becomes very difficult. The hormonal imbalances can also affect egg quality and the uterine lining.

Management is Ongoing:
PCOS cannot be 'cured', but it can be highly managed. The foundation of management is lifestyle: targeted diet (low glycemic index), regular exercise, and maintaining a healthy weight. Medical treatments range from Metformin (for insulin resistance) to Letrozole (to induce ovulation) and, in some cases, IVF.
content.conclusion: If you suspect you have PCOS, do not wait until you want to conceive to seek help. Early management prevents long-term complications like Type 2 diabetes. Book an assessment with Dr. Ankita at Maatritva IVF today.

title: Uterine Fibroids and Pregnancy: What Every Woman Should Know
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Do uterine fibroids affect pregnancy and fertility? Dr. Ankita Mandal explains which fibroids need surgery and which can be left alone. Maatritva IVF Kolkata.

content.h1: Uterine Fibroids, Fertility, and Pregnancy: The Complete Guide
content.intro: Fibroids are extremely common non-cancerous growths in the uterus. Many women panic upon finding out they have them, especially when planning a family. But the reality is: most fibroids do not cause infertility and do not affect pregnancy.
content.body:
Location, Location, Location:
The impact of a fibroid depends almost entirely on its location and, to a lesser extent, its size.

1. Submucosal Fibroids (Inside the cavity):
These grow into the uterine cavity where the baby needs to implant and grow. Even very small submucosal fibroids can act like an IUD, preventing implantation or causing early miscarriage. These almost always need to be removed (usually via hysteroscopy) before trying to conceive or doing IVF.

2. Intramural Fibroids (Within the wall):
These grow within the muscular wall of the uterus. They only affect fertility if they are very large or if they push inward and distort the uterine cavity. Evaluation with a 3D ultrasound or MRI is essential to make this determination.

3. Subserosal Fibroids (Outside the uterus):
These grow on the outer wall of the uterus and protrude outward into the pelvis. They rarely affect fertility and usually do not need treatment before pregnancy.

Fibroids DURING Pregnancy:
If you become pregnant with fibroids, they will need monitored.
- Growth: Fibroids often grow during the first trimester due to increased estrogen levels.
- Pain: Rapid growth can cause a fibroid to outgrow its blood supply ('red degeneration'), causing significant pain. This is managed with rest and pain relief; surgery is avoided during pregnancy.
- Labor and Delivery: Large or multiple fibroids can increase the risk of breech presentation, premature labor, or the need for a Cesarean section (especially if a large fibroid blocks the cervix).

The Surgical Dilemma (Myomectomy):
Removing fibroids (myomectomy) is a major decision. While it can improve fertility for some, surgery itself leaves scar tissue on the uterus, which can slightly increase the risk of uterine rupture during future labor (often necessitating a planned C-section). Dr. Ankita strongly advocates for conservative management unless the fibroid is clearly hindering conception.
content.conclusion: A fibroid diagnosis requires expert, individualised evaluation. Bring your ultrasound reports to Maatritva IVF, and Dr. Ankita will give you a clear, honest assessment of what it means for your fertility.

title: Male Fertility Testing Explained: Beyond Just Sperm Count
author: Dr. Chhabi Ghosh
metaDescription: What does a semen analysis actually test? Learn about sperm count, motility, morphology, and DFI. Comprehensive male fertility guide by Dr. Chhabi Ghosh.

content.h1: Male Fertility Testing Explained: It Is More Than Just 'Sperm Count'
content.intro: When couples face fertility struggles, the focus often immediately shifts to the woman. However, male factor infertility contributes to 40-50% of cases. The cornerstone of evaluation is the semen analysis, but 'count' is only one small part of the story.
content.body:
What a Semen Analysis Really Looks At:
A standard semen analysis (following WHO 2021 criteria) evaluates the sample across several dimensions:

1. Volume: How much semen is produced. Low volume suggests blockage or retrograde ejaculation.
2. Concentration (Count): How many sperm are in each milliliter. Normal is >16 million/mL.
3. Motility: How many sperm are moving (at least 42%) and how well they are moving (progressive motility — swimming forward strongly vs swimming in circles).
4. Morphology: The shape of the sperm. Normal sperm have an oval head, a connecting piece, and a long tail. Even in highly fertile men, 96% of sperm are abnormally shaped. Normal morphology is >4%.
5. Vitality: What percentage of non-moving sperm are actually alive.
6. Liquefaction time: Semen is initially thick and should liquefy within 30-60 minutes to allow sperm to swim.

The Missing Piece: DNA Fragmentation Index (DFI)
A standard semen analysis checks what sperm look like and how they move. It DOES NOT check the genetic cargo inside. Sperm DNA Fragmentation refers to damage or breaks in the DNA strands within the sperm head. A man can have a totally 'normal' semen analysis but very high DFI, which causes IVF failure and recurrent miscarriage. This requires a separate, specialised test.

Preparing for the Test:
For accurate results, abstain from ejaculation for 2 to 5 days before the test. Do not abstain for longer than 7 days, as sperm quality begins to degrade.

What if the results are abnormal?
A single poor semen analysis is not a diagnosis. Sperm fluctuate dramatically based on illness, stress, and heat exposure. It takes ~75 days for new sperm to form. We always recommend repeating the test after 4-6 weeks before finalizing a diagnosis or treatment plan.
content.conclusion: Do not wait months to get the male partner checked. An early semen analysis saves time and stress. Book an evaluation at Maatritva IVF in Newtown Kolkata today.

title: Recurrent Implantation Failure: Why Do Good Embryos Not Stick?
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Recurrent Implantation Failure (RIF) explained. Why do top-quality embryos fail to implant during IVF? Dr. Ankita Mandal explores uterine receptivity and embryo genetics.

content.h1: Recurrent Implantation Failure (RIF): Why Do Good Embryos Not Stick?
content.intro: You had a perfect Day 5 embryo. The lining was optimal. The transfer went smoothly. Yet, the pregnancy test was negative. When this happens repeatedly, it is termed Recurrent Implantation Failure (RIF). Why does it happen, and what can be done?
content.body:
What is RIF?
Generally, RIF is diagnosed when a woman has had 3 or more high-quality embryo transfers (or transfer of at least 4 good-quality embryos in multiple cycles) without achieving a clinical pregnancy.

Implantation relies on a complex dialogue between a healthy embryo and a receptive uterus. If it fails, the problem lies with one or the other — or their interaction.

1. The Embryo: Genetic Abnormalities
The most common cause of implantation failure is a chromosomally abnormal embryo (aneuploidy). Even embryos that look 'Grade A' under the microscope can carry genetic errors that halt their development shortly after transfer. Solution: Preimplantation Genetic Testing (PGT-A) to transfer only euploid (normal) embryos.

2. The Uterus: Structural Issues
Polyps, submucosal fibroids, adenomyosis, or intrauterine adhesions (Asherman's syndrome) act like physical barriers or create a hostile environment. Solution: A diagnostic hysteroscopy allows us to see inside the cavity and correct these issues directly.

3. The Uterus: The Receptivity Window
The endometrium (uterine lining) is only receptive to an embryo for a brief 24-36 hour 'window of implantation.' For about 25-30% of women with RIF, this window is displaced (earlier or later than usual). Solution: The ERA (Endometrial Receptivity Analysis) test determines your exact window, allowing for personalised embryo transfer timing.

4. Undiagnosed Infections (Chronic Endometritis)
A silent, low-grade bacterial infection of the uterine lining (chronic endometritis) causes inflammation that prevents implantation. It has no obvious symptoms. Solution: Uterine biopsy (ALICE test or pathology) and targeted antibiotics.

5. Immunological and Clotting Issues
Overactive natural killer (NK) cells or undiagnosed blood clotting disorders (thrombophilias) can prevent the embryo from establishing a blood supply. Solution: Comprehensive blood tests and treatments like blood thinners or immunosuppressive protocols.
content.conclusion: RIF is heartbreaking, but it usually has a solvable medical cause. Do not simply keep transferring without answers. Dr. Ankita at Maatritva IVF takes a forensic approach to diagnosing and treating RIF.

title: Holistic Ways to Prepare Your Body for IVF
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Holistic preparation for IVF. Diet, supplements, stress management, and acupuncture. Maximize your chances of success with Maatritva IVF, Newtown Kolkata.

content.h1: Preparing Your Body for IVF: A Holistic Approach
content.intro: IVF is a medical marvel, but your body is not a machine. Preparing yourself physically and mentally in the 2-3 months leading up to an IVF cycle can profoundly impact your experience and your outcomes.
content.body:
The 'Pre-Trimester' Matters
The 90 days before egg retrieval are crucial because that is the timeline for a resting follicle to mature into the egg that will be collected. What you expose your body to during this time matters.

1. Nutritional Foundation
Shift heavily toward a Mediterranean-style diet. It is proven to reduce inflammation, which damages egg DNA. Focus on:
- Antioxidant-rich vegetables (berries, leafy greens, brightly coloured peppers)
- Healthy fats (extra virgin olive oil, avocados, walnuts, chia seeds)
- Lean protein (fish, poultry, beans, lentils); reduce red meat and processed meats.
- Minimize refined sugars and alcohol completely.

2. Targeted Supplements (Under Medical Guidance)
Standard prenatal vitamins (with folic acid) are a given. Depending on your diagnosis (e.g., age, PCOS, low AMH), Dr. Ankita may recommend CoQ10 (Ubiquinol), Vitamin D, Omega-3s, or Myo-inositol. Never self-prescribe DHEA or melatonin.

3. Toxin Reduction (Endocrine Disruptors)
Chemicals in our environment can mimic hormones and disrupt the delicate IVF balance. In the months before IVF:
- Switch to BPA-free plastics and glass storage containers.
- Choose phthalate-free, fragrance-free cosmetics and cleaning products.
- Wash all produce thoroughly to reduce pesticide exposure.

4. Movement and Blood Flow
Moderate exercise (walking, swimming, light cycling) increases blood flow to the reproductive organs. However, once stimulation injections begin, switch to very gentle movement (like walking). Intense exercise or twisting (hot yoga) poses a risk of ovarian torsion as ovaries enlarge.

5. Stress and the Cortisol Factor
Stress does not cause infertility, but the process of IVF causes immense stress. High cortisol levels can interfere with reproductive hormones. Find a practice that actively lowers your heart rate: mindfulness meditation, deep breathing exercises, or restorative yoga.
content.conclusion: You cannot control every aspect of IVF, but you can control your preparation. Let the team at Maatritva IVF support you holisticallly as you embark on this journey.

title: What to Expect During the IVF Egg Retrieval Process
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Nervous about your IVF egg retrieval? Dr. Ankita Mandal explains the procedure step-by-step, the anesthesia, and the recovery process at Maatritva IVF Kolkata.

content.h1: What to Expect During the IVF Egg Retrieval Procedure
content.intro: The egg retrieval (ovum pick-up or OPU) is the surgical peak of the first phase of IVF. It is completely normal to be nervous about it, but understanding exactly what happens can significantly reduce anxiety. It is actually a very quick, day-case procedure.
content.body:
Before the Procedure:
You will take your 'trigger shot' exactly 34-36 hours before the scheduled retrieval. This timing is absolutely critical to finalize egg maturation. You will arrive at Maatritva IVF fasting (no food or water for 6-8 hours). 

The Anesthesia:
You will not feel pain during the procedure. At Maatritva IVF, retrievals are performed under short, intravenous general anesthesia (or deep sedation). You will be completely asleep, but because it is not full intubation, you will wake up very quickly once it is over.

The Procedure (Step-by-Step):
1. Positioning: You are positioned as you would be for a routine pelvic exam or transvaginal ultrasound.
2. Cleaning: The vagina is cleaned thoroughly with sterile saline to prevent infection.
3. The Needle: Dr. Ankita uses a transvaginal ultrasound probe equipped with a very fine, hollow needle guide. The needle passes through the vaginal wall directly into the ovaries.
4. Aspiration: The fluid inside each mature follicle is gently suctioned out and collected in test tubes.
5. The Embryology Lab: The tubes are immediately passed through a window to the embryologist, who examines the fluid under a microscope to locate and collect the eggs.
6. Duration: The actual procedure takes only 15 to 30 minutes, depending on the number of follicles.

The Recovery:
You will wake up in the recovery room. Mild cramping (like period pain) and light spotting are normal. You will rest for 1-2 hours while we monitor your vital signs. Once you are fully awake, we will give you something to eat and drink, inform you of the 'egg count', and you can go home.

Post-Retrieval Care at Home:
Rest for the remainder of the day. Use a heating pad and paracetamol for cramps. Stay hydrated with electrolyte fluids. Severe pain, heavy bleeding, or difficulty urinating require immediate medical attention.
content.conclusion: The egg retrieval is a profound milestone in your IVF journey. At Maatritva IVF, our expert anesthetic and clinical team ensures your safety and comfort at every step.

title: Understanding Blastocyst Grading: What Do the Numbers and Letters Mean?
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Confused by embryo grading (like 4AA or 3BB)? Learn exactly how blastocysts are graded and what it means for your transfer success at Maatritva IVF.

content.h1: Understanding Blastocyst Grading: What Does '4AA' Actually Mean?
content.intro: When your embryologist calls to give you an update on Day 5, they often use a combination of numbers and letters—like '4AA' or '3BC'. What sounds like a secret code is actually a standardized way to evaluate the physical appearance (morphology) of a blastocyst embryo.
content.body:
What is a Blastocyst?
A blastocyst is an embryo that has developed for 5 or 6 days after fertilization. By this stage, it has differentiated into two distinct cell types and contains a fluid-filled cavity.

The Grading System Explained:
Most clinics use the Gardner grading system, which consists of a number followed by two letters.

1. The Number (1 to 6): Degree of Expansion
This describes how much the blastocyst has expanded and the size of the fluid cavity.
- 1: Early blastocyst (cavity is less than half the volume of the embryo)
- 2: Cavity is more than half the volume
- 3: Full blastocyst (cavity completely fills the embryo)
- 4: Expanded blastocyst (embryo is larger, and the outer shell is thinning)
- 5: Hatching blastocyst (the embryo is starting to squeeze out of its shell)
- 6: Hatched blastocyst (completely out of the shell)
(Transfer usually involves grades 3, 4, or 5).

2. The First Letter (A, B, or C): Inner Cell Mass (ICM)
The ICM is the group of cells inside the cavity that will eventually become the fetus.
- A: Many tightly packed cells (Excellent)
- B: Several loosely grouped cells (Good)
- C: Very few cells (Fair/Poor)

3. The Second Letter (A, B, or C): Trophectoderm (TE)
The TE is the outer layer of cells that will become the placenta.
- A: Many cells forming a cohesive layer (Excellent)
- B: Fewer cells forming a loose layer (Good)
- C: Very few, large cells (Fair/Poor)

Putting it together: A '4AA' is an expanded blastocyst with a top-quality inner cell mass and a top-quality trophectoderm layer. It has excellent potential for implantation.

Does a 'C' grade mean failure?
No. While 'AA' or 'AB' embryos have the highest statistical chance of implantation, 'BB', 'BC', and even 'CB' embryos absolutely result in healthy babies every day. Also remember, an embryo's physical grade does not guarantee it is genetically normal (only PGT-A testing can show that).
content.conclusion: Embryo grading is a tool, not a crystal ball. Our expert embryologists at Maatritva IVF will explain your embryo report clearly so you feel confident before your transfer.

title: Smoking and Fertility: The True Impact on Men and Women
author: Dr. Chhabi Ghosh
metaDescription: How does smoking really impact fertility in men and women? Learn facts about egg aging, sperm DNA damage, and success rates from Dr. Chhabi Ghosh.

content.h1: Smoking and Fertility: It Is Worse Than You Think
content.intro: Everyone knows smoking is bad for the lungs and heart. But the impact of smoking on fertility—for both men and women—is far more profound and immediate than most couples realize. If you are struggling to conceive, quitting smoking is the single most powerful change you can make.
content.body:
The Impact on Female Fertility:
Smoking accelerates the loss of eggs and accelerates reproductive aging. 
- Chemical Damage: The chemicals in cigarette smoke (nicotine, cyanide, carbon monoxide) speed up the depletion rate of eggs. Once eggs die off, they cannot be regenerated.
- Menopause Timing: Women who smoke reach menopause 1 to 4 years earlier than non-smokers.
- IVF Outcomes: Smokers require higher doses of fertility drugs to stimulate their ovaries, retrieve fewer eggs, experience more canceled cycles, and have a 30% lower IVF pregnancy rate compared to non-smokers. It essentially ages a woman's ovaries by 10 years.

The Impact on Male Fertility:
Sperm are highly vulnerable to oxidative stress caused by smoking.
- Sperm Parameters: Smoking decreases sperm count, reduces motility (swimming ability), and worsens morphology (shape).
- DNA Fragmentation: Most critically, smoking significantly increases Sperm DNA Fragmentation (damage to the genetic code inside the sperm). Sperm with high DNA fragmentation can fertilize an egg, but the resulting embryo often arrests in development or results in early miscarriage.

The Silent Threat: Vaping and E-cigarettes
Many assume vaping is a 'safe' alternative. It is not. While it lacks tar, the nicotine and propylene glycol in e-cigarettes still act as endocrine disruptors, constrict blood vessels (reducing blood flow to the ovaries and testes), and cause oxidative stress.

The Good News: Reversibility
For men, spermatogenesis (creation of new sperm) takes about 72 to 90 days. If you quit smoking today, your sperm quality will show significant improvement in 3 months. For women, while lost eggs cannot be recovered, the inflammatory environment in the ovaries begins to improve immediately upon quitting, leading to improved egg quality in recent cohorts.
content.conclusion: We know quitting is incredibly hard. But stopping smoking before beginning IVF or trying to conceive changes your odds dramatically. Let Maatritva IVF support your whole-health fertility journey.

title: Secondary Infertility: Why Can I Not Get Pregnant Again?
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: Conceived easily the first time but struggling now? Secondary infertility is common but confusing. Understand the causes and when to seek help in Kolkata.

content.h1: Secondary Infertility: When Growing Your Family Becomes Unexpectedly Hard
content.intro: You had no trouble getting pregnant the first time. In fact, it might have been a surprise. So why, when you are tracking cycles and timing everything perfectly for your second baby, is it not happening? This is called secondary infertility, and it is a very real, often isolating experience.
content.body:
What is Secondary Infertility?
Secondary infertility is defined as the inability to become pregnant or carry a pregnancy to term after previously giving birth to a baby without medical assistance. It accounts for nearly 30% of all infertility cases, yet it is rarely talked about.

Why Does It Happen?
The human body changes, and the reproductive system is no exception. Several factors could have shifted since your last pregnancy:

1. Age and Ovarian Reserve: The most common factor. If you had your first child at 32 and are trying for your second at 36, your egg quality and quantity have naturally declined in those four years.
2. Male Factor Changes: Sperm quality can change drastically due to new medications, stress, age, weight gain, or new health conditions like hypertension or diabetes. A previous successful pregnancy does not guarantee current sperm health.
3. Uterine Scarring or Damage: A previous difficult delivery, a C-section (which can leave a uterine scar or 'niche'), fibroid growth, or a condition called adenomyosis can alter the uterine environment, hindering implantation.
4. Pelvic Adhesions or Blocked Tubes: Infections after a previous birth, or the development/worsening of endometriosis, can lead to blocked fallopian tubes.

The Emotional Toll:
Secondary infertility carries a unique emotional burden. Couples often face invalidation from friends and family who say, 'At least you already have one!' This lack of understanding makes the grief confusing and lonely.

When to Seek Help:
The guidelines remain the same: if the female partner is under 35, seek evaluation after 1 year of trying. If over 35, seek help after 6 months. Do not assume that because it worked once, you just need more time. Time is the most critical asset in fertility.
content.conclusion: You do not have to struggle in silence. A simple workup can identify what has changed. Book a consultation with Dr. Ankita at Maatritva IVF, Newtown, to get answers.

title: Varicocele and Low Sperm Count: Is Surgery Necessary?
author: Dr. Chhabi Ghosh
metaDescription: Varicocele is a common cause of male infertility, but does it always need surgery? Dr. Chhabi Ghosh discusses microsurgical varicocelectomy vs IVF options.

content.h1: Varicocele and Male Infertility: Does Every Case Need Surgery?
content.intro: A varicocele is an enlargement of the veins within the scrotum, similar to a varicose vein in the leg. It is one of the most common reversible causes of male infertility. But if you are diagnosed with one, do you have to have surgery before trying for a baby?
content.body:
How Varicocele Affects Fertility:
The testicles need to be slightly cooler than core body temperature to produce healthy sperm. Enlarged varicocele veins pool warm venous blood around the testicles, raising the temperature. This heat stress can cause:
- Lower sperm count
- Decreased sperm motility (movement)
- Increased Sperm DNA Fragmentation (DFI)
- Lower testosterone production over time

Not All Varicoceles Are Equal:
Many men have varicoceles and father children without issue. They are graded clinically from Grade 1 (small, palpable only when bearing down) to Grade 3 (large, visible through the skin). 

When is Surgery (Varicocelectomy) Recommended?
Microsurgical varicocelectomy is considered when:
- The varicocele is palpable (Grade 2 or 3)
- The couple has documented infertility
- The female partner has normal fertility (or treatable factors)
- Semen analysis shows abnormal parameters or high DNA fragmentation

The goal of surgery is to halt further damage and improve sperm quality. Improvement is typicaly seen 3 to 6 months post-surgery.

When to Bypass Surgery and Go to IVF/ICSI:
Surgery is not always the best path. Bypassing the varicocele and proceeding directly to Assisted Reproductive Technology (IVF with ICSI) might be recommended if:
- The female partner is of advanced maternal age (over 35), where waiting 6 months for sperm improvement is too risky for her egg quality.
- There are severe female factor infertility issues (e.g., bilateral blocked tubes) that require IVF regardless of sperm count.
- Previous varicocele surgery did not improve outcomes.
content.conclusion: The decision between varicocele repair and IVF/ICSI requires looking at the couple as a whole unit, not just the man's ultrasound. Let the team at Maatritva IVF guide you to the most efficient path to parenthood.

title: What is a Chemical Pregnancy? Causes and Coping
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: A chemical pregnancy is a very early miscarriage. Understand why it happens, mostly due to chromosomal errors, and how long to wait before trying again.

content.h1: Understanding Chemical Pregnancy: An Early and Silent Loss
content.intro: You took a home pregnancy test and saw two lines. Joy and planning began. But a few days later, you started bleeding, and a follow-up test was negative. This early loss is often called a 'chemical pregnancy.' Though clinically brief, the emotional impact is very real.
content.body:
What exactly is a Chemical Pregnancy?
A chemical pregnancy is a very early miscarriage that occurs before the 5th week of gestation — well before an ultrasound can detect a gestational sac or fetal heartbeat. It is called 'chemical' because the pregnancy was confirmed only by chemical means (the presence of the hCG hormone in blood or urine), rather than clinical ultrasound.

Why does it happen?
It is crucial to know that a chemical pregnancy is almost never caused by something the mother did or didn't do. You didn't cause it by exercising, working, or feeling stressed.

The vast majority (up to 70%) of chemical pregnancies are caused by random chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo. At the moment of fertilization, the complex combining of DNA experienced an error, leading to an embryo that simply could not develop further. The body recognizes this and stops the pregnancy naturally.

Other less common causes include:
- Inadequate uterine lining
- Low progesterone levels
- Undiagnosed clotting disorders
- Uterine anomalies (like a septum or fibroid in the cavity)

Is it common?
Yes. It is estimated that up to 50% of all first pregnancies result in a chemical pregnancy, though many women never even realize they were pregnant and simply assume their period was a few days late and slightly heavier than usual. Today's highly sensitive early pregnancy tests are making us aware of these very early losses more than ever before.

When can we try again?
Medically, there is typically no need to wait; you can try again on your next cycle. In fact, a chemical pregnancy is a positive sign that fertilization and implantation ARE physically possible. However, take the time you need emotionally.

When to seek investigate further:
If you experience two or more chemical pregnancies (or any consecutive miscarriages), it is time to consult a fertility specialist for a recurrent pregnancy loss panel.
content.conclusion: An early loss is still a loss. Be kind to yourself. If you are experiencing recurrent early losses, Dr. Ankita at Maatritva IVF can investigate and manage the underlying causes.

title: Adenomyosis and Fertility: The 'Sister' Condition to Endometriosis
author: Dr. Ankita Mandal
metaDescription: What is Adenomyosis and how does it impact IVF and fertility? Dr. Ankita Mandal explains the symptoms, diagnosis, and treatment pathways for a healthy pregnancy.

content.h1: Adenomyosis and Fertility: The 'Sister' Condition to Endometriosis
content.intro: Heavy bleeding, severe cramps, and an enlarged, tender uterus. While these sound like typical endometriosis or fibroid symptoms, they often point to a deeply misunderstood condition: Adenomyosis. If you are struggling to conceive, understanding adenomyosis is vital.
content.body:
What is Adenomyosis?
While endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to the uterine lining grows OUTSIDE the uterus, adenomyosis occurs when that tissue grows deep INTO the muscular wall of the uterus itself. This causes the uterine wall to grow thick, enlarged (sometimes described as 'boggy' or 'globular'), and severely inflamed.

How does it affect fertility and IVF?
Adenomyosis impacts the uterus's ability to host an embryo:
